title: Major depressive disorder involves motivational conflicts in emotion regulation in daily life.
abstract: What do individuals with major depressive disorder (MDD) want to achieve when regulating their emotions? The answer has not been clear, given that some evidence suggests they are more motivated and other evidence suggests they are less motivated to feel better, than healthy controls are. Tracking emotion regulation in an ecological momentary assessment study in individuals with MDD (= 94) and in healthy individuals (= 90), and using multilevel modeling, we demonstrated that compared with healthy individuals, those with MDD were more likely to experience motivational conflicts (i.e., they endorsed competing goals) in emotion regulation in daily life. Joint frequency analyses showed that compared with healthy individuals, individuals with MDD wanted to both decrease and increase unpleasant emotions more frequently. They were also more motivated to increase and decrease pleasant emotions. Such motivational conflicts carried negative implications. The more individuals with MDD experienced motivational conflicts in emotion regulation, the more severe their clinical symptoms became over time. In follow-up semistructured interviews on experienced conflict and attraction to sadness, individuals with MDD explicitly reported experiencing conflict in emotion regulation more often than healthy individuals, and being more attracted to sadness. Thematic analyses validated by a large language model revealed that, when individuals with MDD were attracted to sadness, they were more likely to describe it as self-consistent. Healthy individuals were more likely to describe sadness as appropriate or useful in the situation. Motivational conflicts in emotion regulation may exacerbate distress and impair success in emotion regulation in MDD. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).
